items.text:
Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
November 26, 2026
Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.
In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.
And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.
In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.
Music part of Vision 2030
As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.
The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.
A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.
Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.
'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'
Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.
It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.
The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.
The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.
Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.
Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.
"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."
ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.
Hidden for two decades
"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.
Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.
"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."
For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.
In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.
The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

November 26, 2026
"My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was important to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," said Frank-Walter Steinmeier during h
items.text:
President Steinmeier calls for investment in Africa on farewell trip
November 26, 2026
"My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was important to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," said Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that, as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.
"For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in Angela Merkel's administration.
This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.
Germany is competing — not just with China
A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks."
As the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy company REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse: "When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.
Meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.
This shows that there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.
When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey, and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets. The Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.
Vocational training meant to open up new prospects
But such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, one million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years. Germany says there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.
During his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Ivory Coast. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.
There are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair, and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier said in Nairobi.
German SMES also interested in Africa
Vocational training is said to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established. "A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," says Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a company that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran."
"More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's new is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.
During the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he said, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses important raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," the entrepreneur said.
Opportunities for the German auto-makers in Africa?
Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market. "The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," said Audebert.
Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms that there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a new car," said Thill. This would mean that potentially five to ten million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa. Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," the Bosch managing director said.
Not just business: African nations as political partners
Even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier said at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, and Kenya. "These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," the president said.

items.title: French actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged 2018 rape
items.summary:
French actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged 2018 rape
Paris court of appeal dismisses allegations relating to a second incident involving actress Charlotte Arnould.
A Paris court has upheld an order for French actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial on charges of raping an actress at his
items.text:
French actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged 2018 rape
Paris court of appeal dismisses allegations relating to a second incident involving actress Charlotte Arnould.
A Paris court has upheld an order for French actor Gerard Depardieu to stand trial on charges of raping an actress at his Paris home in 2018, his lawyer and judicial sources say.
The Paris Court of Appeal ruled on Thursday that Depardieu should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault against Charlotte Arnould on August 7, 2018.
Defence lawyer Delphine Meillet told The Associated Press news agency that the 77-year-old actor would face trial on one rape charge after the court dismissed allegations relating to a second incident six days later.
Depardieu was charged in 2020 with rape and was ordered to stand trial in 2025, but the cinema icon rejected the allegations and appealed.
Arnould has accused Depardieu of raping her twice in 2018 when she was 22.
“He disputes the decision,” Meillet told AP without specifying whether Depardieu would file a further appeal.
Carine Durrieu Diebolt, a lawyer for Arnould, described the court ruling as a relief for her client.
“She has been waiting for this moment for a long time,” Durrieu Diebolt said. “She is fully prepared for it.”
Depardieu, who has acted in more than 200 films and television series, is the highest-profile figure caught up in France’s response to the #MeToo movement.
The actor has been the subject of multiple sexual assault accusations and charges in recent years.
French police are investigating allegations Depardieu and author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman on camera during a 2018 film shoot.
Last week, he dropped his appeal against an 18-month suspended sentence for sexually assaulting two women during the filming of another movie in 2021.
“I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered,” he said in a written statement.
The Arnould decision, meanwhile, “promises to be historic”, Durrieu Diebolt said.
The rape trial poses a much more serious threat to Depardieu, who could face 15 to 20 years in jail if convicted.
Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century. He became one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for Cyrano de Bergerac and a Golden Globe for Green Card.

- Published

The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 Octo
items.text:
Germany's Freigang banned over drugs test issues
- Published
Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.
The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.
The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.
The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.
The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.
Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.
All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.
This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.
Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.
In a club statement, external, Franfurt said they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".
Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.
Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel said: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.
"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.
"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player."

items.summary:
Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe
November 26, 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he had urged his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to cease "military aggression" in Europe during their talks in China.
"I spent a lot of time talking about th
items.text:
Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe
November 26, 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he had urged his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to cease "military aggression" in Europe during their talks in China.
"I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly," Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.
However, the US president did not specify which European territories he mentioned when communicating with Putin. This week, Poland — a NATO member — accused Russia of deliberately violating its airspace.
Trump added that he believes there is a "strong possibility" of such a deal between Russia and Ukraine. "Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH," he wrote in the post.
Trump and Rutte call for 'peaceful resolution'
Trump's post on Truth Social came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Florida. They issued a joint statement afterward calling on Russia not to expand the war in Ukraine.
"We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War — and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible," the statement said.
Trump's comments represent a shift in tone after he cordially called Putin a friend during their meeting in China last week. Approaching Putin, smiling Trump said, "Who is he? He's my friend." Then he shook hands warmly with the Russian leader.
The echoes of the scene reverberated throughout Ukraine and other European nations, which are worried that Trump might side with Putin.
The US president had said he could end the war in Ukraine on the first day of his second term in office.
Russian refinery on fire after attack
Depite Trump's comments, the war shows no signs of ending, with both Russia and Ukraine continuing their mutual attacks.
A fire broke out on Thursday at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region following a drone attack. The strike caused serious damage, according to a social media post by the company.
According to Reuters, two industry sources estimated that Ukrainian drone attacks have reduced the combined crude processing volumes of Russian oil refineries by 45% since late October.
At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Russia is preparing for a large-scale attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics, and essential services.
Zelenskyy also said that crews are working to restore electricity in six Ukrainian regions after Russia launched ballistic missiles and 113 drones overnight.

Phil Taylor came out of retirement to partner Adrian Lewis for England at Thursday's Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth, but the duo endured a disappointing return, losing all five of their matches; Taylor retired from professional darts in 2018
Thursday 26 November 2026 19:03, UK
Phil 'The Power' Taylor and Adrian Lewis suffered five losses from five matches for England at Thursday's Modus Super Series International Pairs Tournament in Portsmouth.
Taylor, now 66, retired from the competitive circuit in 2018, five years after claiming his 16th and final world title. However, the 16-time world champion returned to action to partner his long-time friend Lewis for the tournament.
Their opening match on Thursday saw them face Scotland's John Henderson and Robert Thornton, with the England pair suffering a narrow 4-3 defeat.
Things failed to improve in their second outing, as Taylor and Lewis were beaten 4-2 by Sweden's Andreas Harrysson and Anton Ostlund.

items.title: How a teen’s death raises questions about Colombia’s security crackdown

items.text:
Bogota, Colombia – On the afternoon of September 13, Marelvis Rodriguez said goodbye to her 18-year-old son for the last time.
Ricardo Martinez left home that day for a cattle ranch, tucked away in the Sierra Nevada mountains of northern Colombia, where he said he had been hired as a day labourer to help vaccinate a herd.
A week later, on the morning of September 21, police stormed the ranch, targeting a top commander of the Conquering Self-Defence Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), a paramilitary force that traffics cocaine to Central America, the United States and Europe.
President Abelardo de la Espriella appeared that night before the media, praising the operation that had ended in the deaths of seven alleged paramilitary fighters and three arrests.
"This is undoubtedly a major blow to this narcoterrorist organisation," he said.
Seven white body bags, laid out near a table full of semi-automatic rifles and ammunition, were presented as evidence of the operation's success. Inside one of the body bags was Martinez.
The raid was one of the most high-profile operations of de la Espriella's security crackdown since he took office in August. He has pledged to wage all-out war against Colombia's armed groups, abandoning the country's peace talks and prioritising military offensives instead.
His iron-fisted strategy, he says, will help to secure peace after more than six decades of internal armed conflict in Colombia.
But the operation, which killed Jose Perez, the ACSN's second-in-command, has prompted allegations that a civilian, Martinez, was killed and falsely presented as a paramilitary fighter.
"My son was not part of any armed group," said Rodriguez. "All I want is for justice to be served and my son's name to be cleared because he had nothing to do with the [ACSN]."
The case has ignited fears of a return to one of the darkest chapters in Colombia's internal conflict: a wave of extrajudicial killings known as the "false positives" scandal.
Between 1990 and 2016, state agents killed more than 7,800 civilians and presented them as enemy fighters, according to Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace, a state tribunal.
"We fear that we could see a resurgence of false positives," said Lerber Dimas, the director of the Human Rights Defenders Platform of Sierra Nevada, an organisation that investigates human rights abuses.
Even politicians have warned of the possibility. Representative Daniel Monroy led a protest in Colombia's Congress to highlight Martinez's death, calling it the "first extrajudicial execution of the Abelardo de la Espriella administration".
"Why are they killing young people and presenting them as combat casualties?" the left-wing congressman asked.
Separately, Monroy posted on social media: "I never thought Abelardo would resort to the 'false positives' so soon."
A tight mother-son bond
Living in the Sierra Nevada mountains was meant to be a safe haven for Rodriguez and her teenage son.
In 2020, Rodriguez lost her jobs as a sales associate at a travel agency and as a mariachi singer during the COVID-19 pandemic.
She decided she needed a fresh start. She sold her home and moved to the rural outskirts of Santa Marta, a popular seaside destination rimmed by the Sierra Nevada. There, in the foothills of the mountain range, she bought a 2.5-hectare (6.2-acre) plot of land.
The very next year, a war broke out between the ACSN and the Gulf Clan, the country's largest drug cartel, as they vied for control of international drug routes.
Her neighbourhood, however, was largely spared the violence. Rodriguez said she occasionally saw armed men passing by her home, but the conflict rarely intruded into her day-to-day life as a farmhand and day labourer.
As a single mother, her primary concern was making ends meet. Martinez, her youngest son, dropped out of school and joined his mother in working to support their two-person household.
They picked up odd jobs, from construction work to coffee harvesting to milking cows.
"Everywhere I went, he went," Rodriguez said. "He worked with me on nearby farms. When we didn't have work, we'd go looking for work. We were always working together."
In recent months, he had begun talking to his mother about the future. He planned to learn English so he could become a tour guide and eventually open a hostel to tap into the region's tourism industry.
For the most part, their lives had been peaceful, Rodriguez said.
That sense of normalcy was shattered on the afternoon of September 21, when news spread on social media that a police operation had taken place near the ranch where her son worked.
Rodriguez dropped everything and rushed to find him.
She found that the authorities had blocked off the road, and as she waited to be let through, she learned that police had targeted the ranch itself. At the suggestion of locals, she went to the forensic institute in a nearby city the next day.
There, officials confirmed that her son had been killed.
The Defence Ministry has not publicly explained what happened during the police operation.
It declined to comment to Al Jazeera, saying that cabinet ministers were not allowed to speak to the media without the president's approval.
The presidency also did not respond to a request for comment.
Unresolved questions
Dimas said he pieced together an account of that day based on interviews with local residents.
According to his sources, armed ACSN members arrived at the ranch in the early morning, seemingly intoxicated and tired after a late-night celebration.
They had stopped to rest before continuing their journey up the mountains.
It was then that the police raided the ranch. According to a witness, police singled out Martinez, who was unarmed and dressed as a civilian, and fatally shot him in the chest.
In the days following the operation, rumours circulated online that Martinez was the son of Freddy Castillo, the ACSN's top commander.

Fofana has been criticised for comments he made in the interview with YouTuber Zach Nani in which he appeared to joke about h
items.text:
Fofana has apologised for interview - Alonso
- Published
Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso says defender Wesley Fofana has apologised for a controversial interview he gave on YouTube.
Fofana has been criticised for comments he made in the interview with YouTuber Zach Nani in which he appeared to joke about his penalty miss in a Carabao Cup shootout defeat at Liverpool.
He did not have permission to hold the two-hour interview, which was aired after Chelsea's humiliating 4-1 defeat at home to rivals Leeds on Saturday, but Alonso said the matter was now "closed".
"It was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it was not right, the moment, it was not right, the content," said the Blues boss, who was speaking before Friday's Premier League match at Nottingham Forest.
"We are here to take things seriously. He's said it will not be repeated. We don't want these kind of things and they won't be repeated."
Alonso refused to confirm whether Fofana had been punished by the club, but said "we have addressed that with him."
Fofana's comments followed criticism from fans of his performances this season, including in last weekend's humiliation at the hands of historic rivals Leeds.
But interviewer Nani defended Fofana against the backlash, saying: "People can clearly see he wasn't happy. He admits he didn't play well and says he needs to improve."
The interviewer also defended Fofana's explanation for putting himself forward to take a penalty against Liverpool, saying the defender believed it was his responsibility as one of the senior players on the pitch.
The 25-year-old France defender has often struggled for form and fitness since completing a £70m move from Leicester City in August 2022.
He has made 81 appearances for the club in four years, but has played nine times under new manager Alonso this season.
In that time Chelsea have struggled with defensive frailty, conceding 20 goals in their 11 Premier League games.
They are eighth in the table after falling to a third defeat in their last four league matches.

items.summary:
Two Italians killed by ‘drone strike debris’ in Kuwait
The Italians were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.
Two Italians have died from their injuries in Kuwait, after being hit by falling debris as authorities said they tried to intercept incoming Iranian drones.
Kuwait’s M
items.text:
Two Italians killed by ‘drone strike debris’ in Kuwait
The Italians were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.
Two Italians have died from their injuries in Kuwait, after being hit by falling debris as authorities said they tried to intercept incoming Iranian drones.
Kuwait’s Ministry of Defence said two other workers, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national, were also wounded in the incident, at what the ministry describes as a “vital site”.
However, Iranian state media quotes the military saying there were no offensive or military operations in the region.
“Given the history of hostile actions and the role of the Zionist regime and American forces in using false flags and regional adventures, these accusations are considered a cover for continuing evil and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region,” said Iranian military spokesperson Sardar Shekarchi.
Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation confirmed its citizens’ deaths, saying, “an explosion caused by a drone attack … occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working,” with Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirming the victims were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.
“Regarding the targeting of a vital site in the country as a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, the two injured Italian nationals have died as a result of their injuries,” said Kuwait’s Defence Ministry. It had earlier said the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified “material damage”.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said the Iranian drone attack happened while the Kuwaiti National Guard and Kuwaiti military were meeting with an Italian delegation that was visiting, including the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, as well as the Italian ambassador to Kuwait.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was informed of the “tragic deaths”.
“On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims’ families,” Meloni wrote on X.
Regional criticism
The countries of the Gulf region “have in one voice said an attack against one is an attack against all and have continued to condemn these attacks as a violation of sovereignty”, but we’ve seen an uptick in attacks since September, said Basravi, reporting from Doha.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned Thursday’s “brutal” attack.
In a statement, Albudaiwi stressed that Iran’s continued attacks on Kuwait, targeting its vital facilities and endangering the lives of civilians, constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.
There was no immediate comment from Iran regarding the attack.
But it was in line with Tehran’s “policy change”, said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from the Iranian capital.
“Increasingly we have heard from the Iranian officials … saying that this state of no war, no peace cannot remain in place forever, and Iran is working on some military options … to break the status quo,” said Serdar.
The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the strait.
Thursday’s deadly attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences to counter drone strikes launched by Iran – the first since early September.

The president of the European Council says eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the new European Central Bank (ECB) pre
items.text:
Spanish economist to become new European Central Bank chief
Economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos was announced after a meeting of eurozone leaders.
The president of the European Council says eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the new European Central Bank (ECB) president.
Antonio Costa also announced that Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier have been recommended as members of the ECB executive board, and noted that this paves the way for the formal appointment of the new European Central Bank leadership by December’s European Union summit.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the first Spaniard to take the role, and succeeds France’s Christine Lagarde at the Frankfurt-based institution at a challenging time for the eurozone.
Currently head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Basel-based forum for the world’s major central banks, the 55-year-old will take over in February, when Lagarde would step down several months before her term expires in October next year.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post. The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.
Diplomats have described the Spanish economist as a “steady hand” to steer the institution, with a reputation for pragmatism and consensus-building.
As the Bank of Spain’s chief economist and later governor, he navigated the aftermath of Spain’s 2010s banking crisis, years of ultra-low inflation, COVID-19 and the 2022 inflation surge that followed the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
He also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for banks.
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.
He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second-most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.

items.text:
Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans
November 26, 2026
Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.
Rival Kurdish factions unite to protest plans
The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.
Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.
Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.
Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.
Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.
The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."
Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."
Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."
Contested region even since 2005 reformation
Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.
Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.
The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.
Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.
Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.
The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.
Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

items.title: As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
items.summary:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.
GTA VI launched as t
items.text:
It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.
GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.
Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”
Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.
“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.
That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.
“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”
As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.
But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.
The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.
This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.
The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.
The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.
“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”
Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”
Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.
“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”
This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.
“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”
GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.
The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest

items.text:
Hundreds of flights cancelled as severe weather disrupts Thanksgiving travel in US
- Published
More than 350 flights in the US have been cancelled so far on Thursday as bad weather coincides with busy travel on the Thanksgiving holiday.
Another 700 flights into, out of, or within the US have been delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
On Wednesday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded all flights heading for Miami International Airport after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway. No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating.
More than 80 million Americans were expected to be traveling this week at the same time the National Weather Service (NWS) has forecast storms along the western and eastern coasts of the US that could bring heavy rain and flooding.
The FAA previously warned that delays across the country would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast. On Wednesday, FlightAware reported more than 6,800 delays and more than 160 cancellations.
The NWS forecast a strong storm will deluge the eastern US coast on Thursday, bringing high winds, heavy rainfall and major coastal flooding.
Ahead of expected severe weather in New Jersey, the state's governor, Mikie Sherrill, declared a state of emergency. Several coastal areas that experienced flooding earlier this autumn could be vulnerable again on Thursday.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
In Miami, some travel delays persist after the FedEx plane incident prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period on Wednesday evening.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".
It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

items.text:
Spanish economist de Cos to succeed Lagarde as head of ECB
Spanish monetary economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos on Thursday was set to replace France's Christine Lagarde as the new head of the European Central Bank (ECB). His nomination comes as the Europe's most powerful financial institution grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and a cost of living crisis.
European leaders on Thursday chose the former head of Spain’s central bank, Pablo Hernandez de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the eurozone.
Agreement on the three posts was reached at a summit in Brussels, said an EU diplomat tasked with communicating for the Irish Presidency and speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to be named. French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed the result on X.
De Cos' nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.
The former Spanish central bank governor and the current general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, will take over when current chief Lagarde steps down ‌early on February 7.
Read moreECB President Christine Lagarde to step down in February 2027, nine months before term ends
The way for him to replace her as the next ECB chief became clear on Thursday after the Netherlands decided to back him, effectively standing down its own candidate Klaas Knot.
The reshuffle comes as the ECB grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and worries that political turmoil in France could trigger broader financial market stress affecting other euro zone countries.
De Cos' appointment hands the top job to a southern European policymaker and ally ‌of former ECB President Mario Draghi, reinforcing expectations that the central bank would ultimately use its firepower to contain any new sovereign debt crisis.
His formal approval will come from a meeting of ambassadors of Eurozone countries on Thursday, ahead of endorsement from the bloc’s leaders.
Steady hand
De Cos, 55, a trained monetary economist, has built a reputation for independent thinking anchored in economic theory, and pragmatism picked up over a decade served in policymaking roles.
He worked in various staff positions at the ECB and the Bank of Spain early in his career before making a rare jump to the policymaking level as governor of the national central bank, serving on the ECB's rate-setting Governing Council.
De Cos is a veteran of crises including Spain's banking sector bailout, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the post-pandemic inflation surge that forced the ECB into its fastest interest rate-hiking cycle on record.
While southern European policymakers are often considered "doves" favouring easier monetary policy, colleagues and ECB watchers say De Cos is pragmatic and a moderate who cannot be boxed into any such category.
ECB policy is decided by the 27-member Governing Council, meaning even the president has limited scope to steer interest rates single-handedly.
In any case, any dovish bias would only be relevant if inflation was slightly above target, and this year's surge in price pressures would force any ECB president to keep raising interest rates.
At 4 percent, inflation is now twice the central bank's target and policymakers speaking on and off the record appear unanimous that a rate hike in December is inevitable.
The path beyond is murky, however. Markets expect just one more upward move, given the recent retreat in oil prices and an expected decline in inflation from the spring, when statistical base effects start knocking year-earlier figures from the data set.
(FRANCE 24 with AP and Reuters)

George Russell says he was "amused" by Max Verstappen’s criticism of him after their feud reignited at the Las Vegas Grand Prix but admits it was "avoidable".
After colliding on track in final practice last weekend, Russell publicly criticised Verstappen following the incident. The Dutchman won the race after an intense battle between them and said afterwards that the Mercedes driver is "far below my level".
The pair have clashed several times on track in the past, most notably engaging in a remarkable war of words following an incident during qualifying at the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had pushed unreasonably hard for him to be penalised.

Speaking on Thursday - back at the Lusail International Circuit almost exactly two years on from that incident - ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, Russell said: "At the end of the day, I guess I stand by what I said after practice.
"But he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn't and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that, and that was reasonably amusing. From my side, just a new race weekend, try and focus on the driving and move on."
Russell was pressed on the saga throughout the FIA press conference and revealed he was perhaps "guilty of being just too open and honest when I speak with you guys [the media]".
"It's all avoidable at the end of the day, and it's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I'm looking to continue. I'm not looking to have poor relationships with people. That's just not really the type of person I am," he said.
"There are lessons just to be taken away from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media because I feel that I'm having more of an open conversation with you guys as opposed to remembering there's a camera.
"There are more people in this room than there are cameras, and I feel like I'm talking to you, but I'm not actually talking to you. I need to remind myself that I'm talking to the camera there that's broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway."

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.
As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Will Fofana face disciplinary action?
Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.
James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.
Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.
Why is he still in the team?
Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?
James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.
Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.
Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.
You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?
The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.
Will Chelsea invest in January?
Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.
James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.
It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.
The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.
The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.
How has Joao Pedro's injury affected Chelsea?
JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?
James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.
Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.
Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

A LILLE SPOT OF BOTHER
Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian.
Lille’s winner came from a similarly unlikely source of goals for the French side, with Aleksandar Pavlovic popping up to score a hilarious own goal that left his Bayern teammates giving him the collective stink-eye as he sank to his knees, head in hands in the traditional mea culpa style. Having seen Ethan Mbappé played clean through courtesy of a lightning-fast Lille counterattack, Pavlovic sprinted back towards his own team’s goal like a cheating spouse who’s just realised they left their phone unlocked on the coffee table. Although his panicked chase looked to be in vain, the German hit pay-dirt when Mbappé rolled his low shot past Bayern goalkeeper Jonas Urbig, only to see it rebound off the foot of the post. Cue Pavlovic, who accidentally stabbed the ball into the gaping goal as he attempted what appeared to be the routine task of putting it out for a corner.
While Pavlovic’s own goal was definitely the funniest Bayern have scored in recent memory, it certainly wasn’t the most embarrassing. That dubious honour goes to assorted club blazers including Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Uli Hoeness and Jan-Christian Dreesen, who have publicly questioned whether Musiala is worth the astronomical wages he is paid, given his struggles with knack and recent diagnosis with a treatable neurological disorder. Rummenigge even went so far as to suggest that if the 23-year-old does not return to top form, the remaining four years of his contract would “no longer be justifiable” and suggested a pay cut might be in order. Asked about this tone-deaf and decidedly mercenary invasion of his teammate’s medical privacy by club officials, Joshua Kimmich gave his superiors both barrels. “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public,” he harrumphed. “It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.” Neither is the shame of being second in the Bundesliga while languishing in 15th place in Bigger Cup Monster Group, but don’t expect anyone in the club boardroom to volunteer to trim their wages accordingly.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Will Unwin from 8pm for hot Big Vase action, including Sunderland 2-1 Jagiellonia, Torreense 1-1 Celtic and Crystal Palace 1-1 Real Sociedad, plus reaction from Celta Vigo 0-1 Bournemouth, Brighton 3-0 Universitatea Craoiva and Hearts 0-3 Monaco.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Stability in a company is having standards. Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough. We have players who are here for four years, [who] can’t speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language. For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English” – Oliver Glasner puts his Nottingham Forest squad’s linguistic skills on blast.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 
 I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner.
 
 The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Mike Wilner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

items.text:
Qatari, Egyptian leaders discuss Gaza ‘ceasefire’ and regional security
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani is in Cairo for an official visit aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations.
Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi have discussed regional tensions and efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire” during talks in Cairo.
El-Sisi received the emir on Thursday at Cairo International Airport upon his arrival for an official visit at the Egyptian president’s invitation. After a reception at the presidential palace, the talks began.
Sheikh Tamim’s visit was aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations across various sectors, including investment and energy, as well as coordinating diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and bolster regional security, Qatar said.
“Today, I discussed with my brother, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the latest developments in the region and the importance of continuing consultations and coordinating joint efforts to address current challenges, in a way that helps safeguard our region’s security and stability and fulfil its peoples’ aspirations for peace and prosperity,” Sheikh Tamim said on X after the meeting.
The two leaders discussed efforts to promote regional stability, Egyptian presidential spokesman Mohamed el-Shenawy said in a statement.
They stressed the importance of “intensifying regional and international efforts to prioritise political solutions and dialogue and prevent tensions from widening”, warning of “serious consequences for regional and international security and stability”, the statement added.
The talks also addressed developments in Palestine with el-Sisi outlining Egypt’s efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire”.
The Egyptian leader emphasised the need for all parties to uphold the agreement, ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip and begin recovery and reconstruction programmes without delay.
Qatar’s Emiri Diwan said in a statement that the two leaders exchanged views on the latest regional and international developments, “particularly the situation in the Gaza Strip and joint mediation efforts to solidify the ceasefire”.
The Egyptian statement said el-Sisi also reaffirmed Egypt’s “full support for the security of Qatar and other Gulf states”, stressing that “the security of the Gulf is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
It also said the two leaders discussed ways to strengthen economic ties and cooperation in areas of mutual interest and they agreed to continue “intensifying political consultations and coordination”.
The meeting was also attended by Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani and other senior officials from both countries.

items.text:
How far-right Vox is winning over young voters ahead of Spain's snap election
Spain's Vox party is winning over many young people ahead of the country's snap election on November 29, particularly men. The far-right party is capitalising on the rising cost of living and anti-immigrant sentiment to expand its once-marginal electoral base.
In Spain, a growing number of young people say they will support the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party in this Sunday's key snap election, according to recent polling.
One of those voters is Andres, a 19-year-old student in Madrid who told the news outlet Infobae that he believed Santiago Abascal, Vox's leader, “is undoubtedly the most logical choice” in the parliamentary election.
Andres is Catholic, believes that life starts at conception, opposes what he calls “LGBT+ ideology” and says he supports the idea of a traditional family.
Read moreSpain's right holds poll lead over Sanchez's Socialists ahead of November 29 snap election
He is among around 23.2 percent of people between the ages of 18 and 24 in Spain who support Vox, according to the latest data from the Spanish Centre for Sociological Research published in November.
That is just above the 22 percent who support Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Partido Socialista Obrero Espanol (PSOE), commonly known in English as just the Socialists.
That is a huge jump from 2023, when only 15.4 percent of people from the same age group voted for Abascal’s party. The same increase has been noted among people between 25 and 34 years old, with polls suggesting that support for Vox has jumped from 15 percent during the last election to 22 percent in 2026.
This marks a turning point for Spain, as for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s fascist government in 1975, the far right could join the country’s government.
Watch moreSpain’s political crossroads, Europe’s wider stakes: Spaniards to vote in key election
The centre-right People’s Party, currently leading in the polls at 31.5 percent, has not ruled out an alliance with Vox.
One reason for this rise in support is because “this is a generation of young people facing significant economic challenges who have never experienced the dictatorship”, explained Maria Elisa Alonso, a political scientist and lecturer-researcher at the Université de Lorraine specialising in Spain.
And because of this, they are drawn to the "narrative that blames immigrants for all the country's problems".
Economic insecurity
Young people in Spain are struggling to become independent. On average, they move out of their parents’ home at about the age of 30, while their counterparts in the rest of the European Union do so at around 26, according to Eurostat.
One key factor behind this divide is soaring rent costs and hurdles to homeownership.
An average renter could pay around €1,170 to rent a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid, according to the real estate portal Idealista. That is nearly half the average gross salary of €2,460, according to Spain's National Institute of Statistics.
Vox has promised to deregulate land use, lower taxes and combat illegal squatting to tackle the problem. But above all else, Abascal’s party has blamed the left and immigrants for the high cost of living.
Immigration has become a key topic on the campaign trail ahead of the general election, spurred by the arrival of more than 70,000 migrants from Morocco in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, in North Africa, in late July. The vast majority of those migrants have since returned home.
Immigration is a regular topic at Vox rallies. At one event, the party's leader Abascal denounced people he claimed lived “off the social benefits that Spaniards need and who have no business being in Spain”. He added that “rapists” and “murderers” should be held “in prisons in their own countries”. And he called for a “remigration” policy to, in his words, “reverse the migrant invasion”.
“Vox’s message is very simple," Alonso said. "There isn’t really a political platform. Everything is the fault of immigration. They conflate immigration with crime."
“It’s a narrative that resonates with these disillusioned young people.”
Social media and masculinism
Vox uses social media to attract young voters, regularly posting short videos on patriotism, national identity, the traditional family and anti-feminist ideology on TikTok, Instagram and X.

A media outlet close to Vox has also been accused of spreading misinformation on social media. According to FRANCE 24’s Observers team, social media users accused immigrants of election fraud after the outlet published an article alleging fraudulent registrations in a town near Madrid.
“There is a lack of critical thinking among some Spanish youth, a difficulty in discerning what is true, what is false, and what amounts to manipulation,” Alonso warned.
There is also a gender divide among Vox supporters. While support for the far-right party has generally increased among young people, men in this group are more likely than women to support Vox.
Around a quarter of male voters under 35 intend to vote for the party, according to a survey by the 40dB institute published by Cadena SER radio.
Only an estimated 20 percent among women of the same age said that they supported Vox.
By contrast, around 32 percent of young women supported Sanchez’s PSOE.
This trend is not unique to Spain, as female voters are more likely than their male counterparts to support progressive views in Europe and in the United States.

The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric ‌‌as his ‘marching orders’.
A United States judge has barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from putting the licences of eight Walt Disney-owne
items.text:
US judge blocks Trump’s FCC attempt to target Disney’s ABC stations
The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric ‌‌as his ‘marching orders’.
A United States judge has barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from putting the licences of eight Walt Disney-owned ABC TV stations up for early review, a blow to President Donald Trump’s efforts to rein in US media companies.
US District Judge Loren AliKhan, in Washington, DC, granted Disney’s request for a preliminary injunction on Wednesday. The injunction barred the FCC from holding a hearing on the licences, a step that could have led to their revocation and forced the stations off the air.
“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote, saying the FCC appeared to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign, driven by Trump, that threatened the broadcaster’s free-speech rights.
AliKhan, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, said ABC had detailed “a campaign of retaliation against them in response to their exercise of their First Amendment rights,” which on its own is an ‘irreparable injury’”.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whom Trump named to the position in January 2025, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”, the judge added.
A spokesperson for ABC News said, “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment.”
Carr ordered reviews of licences ‌for the eight stations in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, even though the renewals were not due to be considered until October 2028 at the earliest. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.
Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August to block the early review of the stations in Los Angeles, Chicago, New York and other cities, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over broadcast content in violation of the US Constitution.
In response to AliKhan’s decision, an FCC spokesperson has said that the granting of the injunction was “wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.”
They added, “We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”
Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programmes that he dislikes or that have been critical of him or his administration.
Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations are extremely rare, critics said that the risk of losing a licence could have a chilling effect on a broadcaster and raise concerns about government interference.
Trump has waged aggressive attacks on the news media, and the latest move follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney.
In July, Trump repeated a call for ABC stations to lose their licences because the network refused to air a prime-time speech he gave that said US elections are vulnerable to fraud.
In reacting to the judicial decision, Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said the ruling “brings ‌‌badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicised the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control”.
The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show “The View,” which discusses US politics, after saying it may be subject to federal rules requiring broadcasters ‌‌to ‌‌provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.
Disney previously said that as a result of that investigation, the programme did not invite any political candidates to appear before the November midterm elections, and the broadcaster cited the FCC’s “pressure campaign”.
